egg-omelet-or-scrambled-egg-with-cheese-.title: Egg omelet or scrambled egg with cheese and meat, no added fat

content.title: About
content.content: The dish consists of eggs, lean meat (e.g., chicken breast or ham), cheese and seasonings. It is prepared without added oil or other fats, making it a low‑calorie source of protein.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Eggs are one of the most nutrient‑dense foods, containing all essential amino acids.
A modest amount of cheese increases calcium and vitamin D bioavailability.
Lean meat adds extra B‑vitamins, especially B12.
The meal is popular among athletes and weight‑watchers for its high protein and low calorie profile.
Cooking without fat preserves the natural flavors of the ingredients and reduces oxidized fat formation.

items.title: High protein content
items.content: Eggs and meat provide a complete amino acid profile that supports muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: B2, B6 and B12 support energy metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Source of minerals
items.content: Provides iron, zinc and phosphorus, important for blood formation, immunity and bone health.

items.title: Low carbohydrate
items.content: Suitable for low‑carb diets and blood‑sugar control.

items.title: Satiety support
items.content: The combination of protein and a small amount of cheese helps maintain fullness for longer periods.

items.title: Egg or dairy allergy
items.content: Individuals with allergies may experience reactions up to anaphylaxis.

items.title: Cholesterol content
items.content: Eggs contain cholesterol; people with hypercholesterolemia should monitor intake.

items.title: Sodium in meat and cheese
items.content: Excess salt can raise blood pressure; choose low‑sodium lean options.

items.title: Meat quality
items.content: Use fresh, reputable sources to avoid food‑borne illness.

content.title: How to Cook
content.content: Beat the eggs, add diced lean meat and grated cheese, season with salt and pepper. Pour the mixture onto a pre‑heated non‑stick pan and cook over medium heat, stirring until the eggs set but remain moist.

content.title: Storage
content.content: The dish is best eaten fresh. If needed, store in a sealed container in the refrigerator for up to 24 hours. Reheat in a pan without adding oil.

content.title: About
content.content: Fish are aquatic vertebrates that serve as a valuable source of high‑quality protein, omega‑3 fatty acids, vitamins, and minerals. Depending on the species, fish can have a delicate or firm flavor and a variety of textures. They are widely used in cuisines around the world.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Fish contain all essential amino acids required by humans.
Omega‑3 fatty acids EPA and DHA found in fish support heart and brain health.
The fastest fish, the sailfish, can reach speeds over 100 km/h.
Some fish species, such as salmon, can change sex during their lifetime.
Fish are often used in traditional medicine to improve vision and reduce inflammation.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Fish provides high‑quality protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Omega‑3 fatty acids
items.content: EPA and DHA help maintain cardiovascular health, lower triglycerides, and support brain development.

items.title: Vitamin D
items.content: Fatty fish are one of the few natural food sources of vitamin D, important for bones and immunity.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Fish supplies iodine, selenium, zinc, and iron, which are vital for metabolism and hormonal balance.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: Compared with red meat, fish contains less saturated fat, making it a heart‑friendly option.

items.title: Fish allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to fish, ranging from skin rashes to anaphylaxis.

items.title: Heavy‑metal contamination
items.content: Certain large predatory fish can accumulate mercury and other toxins; intake should be limited.

items.title: Food poisoning
items.content: Improperly stored or undercooked fish can harbor bacteria and parasites that cause illness.

items.title: High sodium in canned fish
items.content: Canned fish often contains added salt, which may be problematic for people with hypertension.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Fish can be steamed, baked, grilled, fried, boiled, or eaten raw as sushi or sashimi. It pairs well with lemon, herbs, olive oil, and vegetables. For a softer texture, fish can be marinated or poached in broth.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store fresh fish in the refrigerator at 0‑2 °C in an airtight container for up to 2 days. Keep frozen fish at –18 °C; when properly stored it retains quality for up to 6 months. Before cooking, check the smell—fresh fish should have a mild, clean scent without ammonia notes.

content.title: About
content.content: Beef gravy is a thick, savory sauce made by reducing beef stock, meat drippings, and fat, often seasoned with herbs and aromatics. Traditionally it is prepared from beef bones, meat, onion, and carrot, simmered for several hours, then strained to achieve a smooth, flavorful liquid used to enhance dishes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Beef gravy has been a staple of British cuisine since the 19th century as a way to use pan drippings.
Classic recipes call for slow simmering of bones for 6+ hours to extract collagen and gelatin.
In the United States, gravy is commonly served with turkey at Thanksgiving, though the original version is beef-based.
A "brown gravy" variant often includes soy sauce or caramelized sugar for deeper color.
Prepared gravy can be frozen in portion-sized cubes for quick future use.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Gravy provides a notable amount of protein from beef, supporting muscle maintenance.

items.title: Source of iron
items.content: Beef stock is high in heme iron, which is readily absorbed by the body.

items.title: Contains collagen
items.content: Long simmering releases gelatin that turns into collagen when cooled, beneficial for skin and joints.

items.title: Low in carbohydrates
items.content: Gravy contains virtually no carbs, making it suitable for low‑carb diets.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: The cooking process retains B12 and B6 vitamins, important for nervous system function and metabolism.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Store‑bought or heavily seasoned gravy can be very salty; people with hypertension should watch portions.

items.title: Fat content
items.content: Traditional recipes include beef fat, increasing calories and saturated fat levels.

items.title: Beef allergy
items.content: Some individuals may have an allergic reaction to beef proteins.

items.title: Bacterial growth if mishandled
items.content: Leaving gravy at room temperature for more than 2 hours can promote bacterial contamination.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve hot gravy over roasted meats, mashed potatoes, vegetable casseroles, or baked potatoes. It can be stirred into sauces, stews, or used as a base for soups. For a creamier texture, thin with milk or cream.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Cool gravy to room temperature, then transfer to an airtight container. Refrigerate up to 4 days or freeze in portion‑size bags for up to 3 months. Reheat to a rolling boil before serving to ensure safety.

green-peas-canned-reduced-sodium-cooked-.title: Green peas, canned, reduced sodium, cooked with oil

content.title: About
content.content: Canned green peas with reduced sodium, cooked in vegetable oil, are a ready‑to‑eat product made from fresh peas that are blanched, seasoned with salt and oil, then sealed in an airtight can.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Green peas belong to the legume family and are a good source of plant protein.
Canning preserves the peas' nutrients and flavor for long periods without refrigeration.
Reduced sodium makes the product more suitable for people monitoring their salt intake.
Canned peas are often used in quick dishes such as soups, stews, and salads.
Cooking in oil enhances the absorption of fat‑soluble vitamins.

items.title: Rich in plant protein
items.content: Peas provide about 5 g of protein per 100 g, supporting muscle maintenance.

items.title: Source of dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber aids digestion and helps maintain satiety.

items.title: Low sodium content
items.content: Reduced salt levels are beneficial for blood pressure control.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Peas contain thiamine, folate, and vitamin B6, important for metabolism.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: The product supplies iron, magnesium, and phosphorus, supporting energy production and bone health.

items.title: Legume allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to peas.

items.title: Oil content
items.content: The added oil adds calories, which may be a concern for low‑calorie diets.

items.title: Sodium presence
items.content: Although reduced, the product still contains salt and may not be suitable for strict sodium‑free diets.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Peas can be eaten straight from the can, added to soups, stews, salads, pasta dishes, or used as a sandwich filling. For extra flavor, briefly sauté with herbs and spices.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store unopened cans in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. After opening, keep the peas in a sealed container in the refrigerator and consume within 3–4 days.

content.title: About
content.content: The opossum is a small marsupial native to North and South America. It is known for its ability to “play dead” when threatened. Opossums have a fur‑covered body, a long tail, and sharp teeth that allow them to eat both plant and animal matter.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Opossums are the only marsupials that live in North America.
They have a continuous tooth replacement system: baby teeth fall out and permanent teeth keep growing.
Opossums possess a natural resistance to the venom of cobras and some other poisonous snakes.
Unlike most mammals, opossums have a third eyelid that protects their eyes while feeding.
They can perform “thanatosis” – feigning death – to deter predators.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Opossum meat provides a high amount of complete protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Low fat content
items.content: Compared with many other game meats, opossum meat is relatively low in fat, making it a lean dietary option.

items.title: Rich in iron
items.content: The meat is a good source of heme iron, which is more readily absorbed than plant‑based iron.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: It contains B12, B6, and niacin, supporting nervous system function and metabolism.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Opossum meat supplies zinc and phosphorus, important for immune health and bone strength.

items.title: Parasite risk
items.content: As with other wild game, opossums can carry parasites and diseases, so the meat must be thoroughly cooked.

items.title: Allergic reactions
items.content: Some individuals may develop an allergy to marsupial meat.

items.title: Organ toxicity
items.content: Liver and kidneys can accumulate toxins; it is advisable to avoid these organs.

items.title: Stress hormone content
items.content: Wild animals may have elevated cortisol levels, which can affect flavor and potential effects.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Opossum meat is commonly grilled, stewed, or pan‑seared as steaks. It should be marinated before cooking to mellow the flavor. In some cuisines it is used in sausages and pâtés.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store fresh meat in the refrigerator at 0 °C–4 °C for no more than 2 days. For longer storage, freeze it in an airtight bag at –18 °C; it keeps well for up to 6 months. Thaw frozen meat in the fridge before cooking.

pasta-whole-grain-with-tomato-based-sauc.title: Whole Grain Pasta with Tomato Sauce and Vegetables, Ready-to-Heat

content.title: About
content.content: Whole grain pasta with tomato-based sauce and added vegetables is a ready‑to‑heat meal. It contains whole‑grain pasta, tomato sauce, carrots, broccoli, bell pepper and spices. The dish is rich in fiber, B‑vitamins, vitamin C and antioxidants.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Whole‑grain pasta provides more fiber and micronutrients than refined white pasta.
The tomato sauce is made from ripe tomatoes, a rich source of lycopene, an antioxidant.
Vegetables are added after the pasta is cooked to preserve crunch and nutrients.
The meal can be stored in the refrigerator for up to 5 days and frozen for up to 2 months.
Heat in a microwave for 2‑3 minutes or on the stovetop, stirring occasionally.

items.title: High in Fiber
items.content: Whole‑grain pasta supplies dietary fiber that supports healthy digestion and satiety.

items.title: Vitamins and Minerals
items.content: Tomatoes and vegetables provide vitamin C, vitamin K, potassium and folate, supporting immunity and heart health.

items.title: Low Glycemic Index
items.content: Whole‑grain pasta releases glucose more slowly, helping to maintain stable blood sugar levels.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Lycopene from tomatoes and carotenoids from carrots protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Sustained Energy
items.content: Complex carbs from whole grain and protein from vegetables give lasting energy.

items.title: Gluten Allergy
items.content: Wheat‑based pasta contains gluten, which can trigger reactions in people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Sodium Content
items.content: The tomato sauce may contain added salt; individuals monitoring sodium intake should account for this.

items.title: Food Additives
items.content: Some versions may include preservatives; check the label if you have specific intolerances.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Heat the meal in a microwave or on the stovetop, stirring until evenly warm. Serve as a standalone dish or top with Parmesan, fresh herbs, or a drizzle of olive oil.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep refrigerated at 0‑4 °C in an airtight container for up to 5 days. For longer storage, freeze at –18 °C and reheat directly after thawing.

ravioli-cheese-and-spinach-filled-with-c.title: Ravioli, cheese and spinach-filled, with cream sauce

content.title: About
content.content: Ravioli are small pasta parcels filled with a mixture of cheese and spinach, served in a smooth cream sauce. The durum‑wheat dough gives a firm bite, while the filling adds a buttery, slightly nutty flavor with a hint of spinach bitterness.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The tradition of stuffing ravioli with cheese and greens originated in Italy, especially in the Lazio and Tuscany regions.
Cream sauce is typically made from heavy cream, butter, and Parmesan, giving the dish a golden hue and velvety texture.
Spinach retains most of its vitamins when lightly sautéed before being mixed with cheese.
Ravioli can be made at home or produced industrially; the latter are often flash‑frozen for long‑term storage.
In Italy, ravioli are sometimes finished with a sprinkle of fresh basil or parsley for added brightness.

items.title: Rich in calcium
items.content: The cheese filling provides a good source of calcium, essential for strong bones and teeth.

items.title: Source of iron
items.content: Spinach contributes iron, which is necessary for oxygen transport in the blood.

items.title: Contains vitamin K
items.content: Vitamin K from spinach supports blood clotting and vascular health.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: Combined cheese and wheat pasta deliver complete protein useful for muscle maintenance.

items.title: Potential probiotics (when using cultured cream)
items.content: If the cream sauce is prepared with cultured cream, it may help promote a healthy gut microbiome.

items.title: Dairy allergy
items.content: Cheese and cream can trigger allergic reactions in individuals with lactose intolerance or milk‑protein allergy.

items.title: High calorie content
items.content: The cream sauce and cheese make the dish calorie‑dense; portion control is advised for weight‑conscious diets.

items.title: Sodium levels
items.content: Cheese often contains salt; those monitoring sodium intake should choose low‑salt or reduced‑fat varieties.

items.title: Gluten
items.content: The wheat dough contains gluten, making the dish unsuitable for people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the ravioli hot, drizzled with cream sauce. Garnish with grated Parmesan, fresh herbs, or toasted pine nuts. Pairs well with a light white wine or a delicate red.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep cooked ravioli in an airtight container in the refrigerator for 2‑3 days. Frozen ravioli retain quality for up to 3 months; thaw in the fridge before reheating.

spaghetti-sauce-with-meat-and-added-vege.title: Spaghetti sauce with meat and added vegetables

content.title: About
content.content: Spaghetti sauce with meat and added vegetables is a ready‑to‑heat tomato‑based sauce enriched with chunks of beef, pork or turkey and mixed vegetables such as carrot, celery and sweet pepper. It has a deep aroma, a slightly sweet flavor and works well as a base for pasta, casseroles and other Italian‑style dishes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The sauce contains about 15 % vegetables by weight, boosting its nutritional value.
The recipe is derived from the classic Italian Bolognese sauce, but modern versions often use leaner cuts of meat.
Industrial production involves slow simmering to preserve flavor and improve meat texture.
Typical spice blend includes basil, oregano, garlic and black pepper, enhancing the taste profile.
The sauce is packaged in glass or plastic jars and remains stable for up to 12 months when stored in a cool place.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: The meat provides high‑quality protein essential for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: Meat and vegetables supply vitamin B6, niacin and riboflavin, which support energy metabolism.

items.title: Lycopene and antioxidants
items.content: Tomatoes are rich in lycopene, an antioxidant that helps protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Dietary fiber
items.content: Added vegetables contribute soluble and insoluble fiber, promoting healthy digestion.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: The sauce provides potassium, iron and magnesium, important for heart and muscle function.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Prepared sauces can be high in salt; people monitoring sodium intake should limit portions.

items.title: Meat allergy
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic or intolerant to specific types of meat used in the sauce.

items.title: Preservatives
items.content: Certain versions contain food preservatives; those with sensitivities should choose preservative‑free options.

items.title: Added sugar
items.content: A small amount of sugar is sometimes added for balance, which may be a concern for diabetics.

content.title: How to Use
content.content: Heat the sauce and toss with cooked spaghetti, stuffed pasta, lasagna or use it as a base for stews. Finish with fresh herbs or grated cheese before serving.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the unopened jar in a cool, dry place. Once opened, keep refrigerated and consume within 5 days. For longer storage, freeze in an airtight container for up to 3 months.

turkey-dark-meat-roasted-skin-eaten.title: Turkey, dark meat, roasted, skin eaten

content.title: About
content.content: Dark turkey meat is the portion of the bird that contains more myoglobin than white meat, giving it a richer flavor and darker color. When roasted with the skin on, it stays juicy and flavorful, while the crisp skin adds a pleasant texture. Turkey is a popular source of lean protein, widely used in both festive and everyday dishes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Dark meat comes mainly from the thigh and drumstick, where the muscles work harder than in the breast.
Turkey skin contains beneficial fats that help absorb fat‑soluble vitamins.
Roasting with the skin helps retain moisture, making the meat more tender.
Turkeys were domesticated by Native Americans over 2,000 years ago.
In the United States, turkey is traditionally associated with Thanksgiving.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Dark turkey meat provides about 25 g of protein per 100 g, supporting muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Contains iron
items.content: Higher myoglobin levels mean better iron content, important for blood formation.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Turkey is high in B12, niacin (B3) and B6, which support nervous system function and metabolism.

items.title: Healthy fats in the skin
items.content: The skin supplies monounsaturated and polyunsaturated fatty acids that can benefit heart health when eaten in moderation.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: Compared with red meat, turkey has less saturated fat, making it a better choice for low‑fat diets.

items.title: Food‑borne illness risk
items.content: Undercooked dark meat may harbor pathogens like Salmonella. Cook to an internal temperature of 74 °C (165 °F).

items.title: Poultry allergy
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to turkey proteins.

items.title: High sodium in processed products
items.content: If the turkey is brined or smoked, it can contain a lot of salt, which is a concern for hypertension.

items.title: Calorie density of the skin
items.content: The skin adds extra calories and fat, so those watching weight should moderate its intake.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Roasted turkey with skin can be served whole, sliced thin for sandwiches, added to salads, or incorporated into hot dishes like pasta and risotto. The skin can be eaten crispy or removed for a leaner option.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cooked turkey in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. For longer storage, freeze portions in a zip‑top bag with the air removed – they keep well for 2‑3 months. Reheat to an internal temperature of 74 °C before serving.
